result:
**The final search score is 0.5588, against 0.365 for LRU, and I used 9 of the 24 scorer calls.** The answer is in `final.py`.

| | Search score (official) | My local held-out seeds |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline (LRU) | 0.365 | — |
| First best: W-TinyLFU | 0.533 | 0.466 |
| Final pick: W-TinyLFU tuned by shadow caches | **0.5588** | **0.522** |

The held-out column comes from my own synthetic traces with seeds I never tuned on. The official held-out score is taken later on traces I haven't seen. My traces model hot keys, loops, one-off scans, popularity shifts, mixes and recency-heavy patterns.

**Why it beats LRU:**
- **The base policy is W-TinyLFU.** New keys go into a small recently-used area first. A key only moves into the main cache if it has been requested more often than the key it would push out. This stops one-off scans from flushing hot keys, and when a loop is longer than the cache it keeps a fixed part of the loop instead of missing on every request.
- **It tunes itself to the current traffic.** About 24 small simulated caches run in the background, each with a different setting:
  - how big the recently-used area is: 1–80%;
  - how much of the main cache is protected: 0.8 or 0.3;
  - how fast old request counts fade.

  Each one sees about a quarter of the keys, picked by hashing the key, and its size is scaled down to match. The real cache copies the settings of whichever simulation has the best recent hit rate, and only switches when the leader is at least 1% ahead.
- **Effect:** the plain W-TinyLFU did badly on the recency trace (0.716 vs ARC's 0.847). This version reaches 0.845 there without losing ground on the loop and scan traces.

**Other approaches I measured:**
- **ARC:** 0.407. It does well on recency and badly on loops.
- **W-TinyLFU that adjusts its area size by trial and error over time:** better on recency locally but worse elsewhere, so I dropped it.
- **Shadow caches that see every key (0.552) or half the keys (0.5585):** about as good, but two to four times more expensive to run.
- **Allowing ties into the main cache, other grids and other timing constants:** no change on my traces.

**Notable step:** my first quarter-sampled version lost a lot on the official shifting-loops trace (0.698 → 0.565). The cause was a weak hash for choosing which keys the simulations see. With a properly mixing hash it recovered to 0.685, at a quarter of the cost of the full simulations.

**Candidate log (local score is on my tuning seeds):**

| Candidate | Local score | Official | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| lru | 0.349 | 0.365 | baseline |
| arc | 0.388 | 0.407 | dropped |
| wtlfu | 0.457 | 0.533 | first best |
| trial-and-error W-TinyLFU | 0.466 | — | dropped |
| shadow (all keys) | 0.494–0.503 | 0.552 | best at the time |
| shadow3 (quarter of keys, weak hash) | 0.516 | 0.537 | lost on shifting loops |
| shadow4 (switches only at 1% lead) | 0.524 | 0.536 | dropped |
| shadow4r2 (half of keys) | 0.526 | 0.5585 | good but expensive |
| shadow5 (quarter of keys, good hash) | 0.526 | 0.554 | kept |
| **shadow6 (pruned grid, 3 fade speeds) = final** | **0.528** | **0.5588** | **final** |
| shadow7 and other tuning sweeps | flat | — | dropped |

On my traces, the biggest gap to the perfect-hindsight limit is shifting loops (0.35 vs 0.60). None of the fixed settings I tried did much better there, so closing that gap would need a different kind of policy.

**Speed:** the 8-second limit is a real concern. On my traces this takes about 2.5 s for 640k requests when the laptop is quiet. It slowed by up to about 5× while the machine was busy, and one sweep ran about 57 s, well past the 20-second guideline. The official runs passed, but I can't see how long the unseen traces will be.
